Some initial observations were made on the pollination strategies of Acanthus ilicifolius by Primack et al. (1981). Flowers of Queensland plants are adapted for cross-pollination rather than self-pollination, although the latter can occur. While pollen is present from opening of the flower, the stigma does not become receptive until the flower has been open for a full day. The pollinator (Yellow-breasted Sunbirds, and probably Xylocopa bees) in probing for nectar at the base of the flower, separates the two pairs of stamens, allowing the stigma to descend and pick up previously deposited pollen from its back. When the pollinator withdraws from the flower the anthers come together again and pollen is deposited on its back. Duke (2006) also suggested that the chief pollinators in Australia are the bees. Aluri et al. (2017) also investigated the pollination of A. ilicifolius in India, indicating that flowers were visited by Xylocopa and blue-banded (Amegilla cingulata) bees, a wasp species (Odynerus sp.) and a butterfly species (Borbo cinnara); all of these genera occur in Australia. In keeping with the findings of Primack et al. (1981), their study confirmed that pollination was most effective when carried out by bees. Fruits take about a month to mature and, as with many Acanthaceae species, are flung out when the capsule explodes in response drying. They can be dispersed up to 2 m and can presumably be further dispersed by tidal movements. They germinate in the wet season (Aluri et al. 2017). After clearing of mangroves in India, Acanthus ilicifolius becomes dominant (Aluri et al. 2017) forming large patches by both vegetative means and from seed.

Part of the mangrove association of northern Australia. Duke (2006) indicates that Acanthus ilicifolius occupies an intermediate upstream estuarine position where salinity is less than sea water but not affected by freshwater, and its inundation frequency from tides varies from high to low indicating that it is tolerant of inundation from less than 20 times per month to more than 45 times per month. They can form "dense frontal thickets" or exist as patches in the understory up to the high water margin.

Acanthus ilicifolius is a mangrove species found from India, throughout Malesia extending to the Solomon Islands, New Hebrides and New Caledonia. It has apparently been introduced into South Africa (Clarke 1912). In Australia it is found along the tropical coastlines in saline tidal areas from the Daly River in the Northern Territory east to the Fitzroy River in Queensland (Duke 2006).

Cotyledons c. 14--21 × 18--21 mm, rather thick and fleshy, base auriculate. First pair of leaves with toothed or smooth margins. At the tenth leaf stage: leaf margin armed with spines or pungent points. Stems clothed with purple, slightly raised glands. Seed germination time 27 to 41 days.

The majority of Australian populations of Acanthus ilicifolius have been collected with toothed leaves and axillary spines, but specimens with entire leaves and lacking axillary spines do occur. Chinese Violet plants spread by seed and plant fragments, and can flower and fruit year round. The seeds are dispersed explosively from the drying fruit capsules. After most of the ripe capsules have released their seeds, the plant dies back to ground level. Winter frosts kill above-ground plant parts but plants regrow the following spring from their basal shoots. Trailing stems can take root at each node when they come into contact with moist soil. Most infestations in Australia have occurred as a result of dumping garden waste or uncontrolled garden plantings growing into nearby areas.

Asystasia gangetica subsp. micrantha is native to tropical Africa and Arabia, as well as South Africa, Madagascar and the Mascarene Islands. It has been introduced relatively recently into Asia where it is recorded from Malaysia, Singapore and China as well as Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Australia. It was first brought to attention in Australia in New South Wales from Boat Harbour, north of Newcastle in 1999. The taxon is presently known from disjunct localities in the Gold Coast and Shoalwater Bay areas in Queensland and from Rapid Creek in Darwin in the Northern Territory (Skinner 2015, Westaway et al. 2016); also recorded for Christmas Island, viz. Brillantaisia lamium spreads by seeds and by layering. The long capsules each produce about 30 seeds and these are flung out of the capsule when it explodes in response to wetting or drying. The seeds are covered with hairs that in the dry state are pressed to the surface, but on wetting these expand and exude a mucilage which probably glues the seed to a surface as it dries again. As with other Acanthaceae species, all nodes are capable of forming roots and so any stem fragments or sprawling plants are capable of taking root (Barker 2007). It can disperse further than the local area by water and as contaminant of vehicles, machinery and nursery stock (Grice & Setter 2003).

Brillantaisia lamium's preference is for wetter and shaded areas where it will eventually form dense mats of vegetation because of its sprawling habit. In Australia it has been found growing along the edges of waterways, in orchards, in nurseries and around sugarcane plantations and it is able to grow in shade. Where there is plentiful moisture it has the potential to invade disturbed areas such as roadsides, agricultural clearings and gaps in forests. It is a known troublesome weed forming dense stands beneath tropical African crops such as coffee, oil-palm, bananas and rubber.

Brillantaisia lamium is native to wet forest regions of Africa, from Sierra Leone on the west coast to Ethiopia, almost on the eastern coast and then south to Tanzania and northern Angola. In Australia it was first collected from the Innisfail area in northern Queensland in 1996 but is now also known from Alexandra Bay near Daintree and from rainforest margins at Whyanbeel Creek, where, in 2000, it was described as a common weed. Graptophyllum pictum is cultivated throughout the world, usually as the 'Caricature Plant'. New Guinea has been proposed as the home of G. pictum and here it has been recorded from logged-over forest and rainforest undergrowth as a tree but it is also often grown as an ornamental or as a hedge plant around villages. Following clearing of part of the Buderim population in the early 2000s many G. reticulatum plants resprouted, and fruit and prolific flowering were observed (Shapcott 2000, Lynch 2007). Graptophyllum reticulatum is a slow-growing shrub with a juvenile period estimated at over two years and a lifespan of over 30 years. It regenerates through resprouting and possibly from a short-lived seed bank. Viable seed has only been recorded by Shapcott (2000) while MacIntyre (in Lynch 2007) indicated that those seeds which were produced tended to be eaten and bored into by insects. While there is little recruitment from seed in the wild, garden-grown species of Graptophyllum, such as G. ilicifolium, can produce dozens of self-sown seedlings each year (I. Champion, pers. comm. in Lynch 2007). The population genetics of Queensland’s Graptophyllum species were investigated by Dr A. Shapcott, University of the Sunshine Coast (Shapcott 2005), who found: (i) All four species have quite high levels of genetic diversity, although G. reticulatum has the lowest diversity. (ii) All species were significantly inbred but G. reticulatum was the most inbred. (iii) Genetic differentiation between populations was highest in G. reticulatum. The crowded inflorescences of Hypoestes aristata mean that at any one time there are usually a large number of flowers with their associated nectar and pollen available, and studies in Africa (Padyšáková et al. 2013) have documented 15 different visitors ranging from sunbirds to various insect representatives. Individual flowers last up to five days and during this time they produce nectar which accumulates in the narrow, c. 1 cm long corolla tube. The lilac-purple flowers with their paler-coloured nectar guide at the base of the upper lip and their exserted style and stamens would suggest insect pollination and two carpenter bee species (Xylocopa spp.) were found to be the most effective pollinators, leading to seed formation, while none of the other visitors were of the right size to achieve this and were basically nectar robbers. This latter category included the sunbirds and the honeybees. Further observations by the same group (Tropek et al. 2013) indicated that where there were large populations of H. aristata flowers the sunbirds would prevent the carpenter bees from accessing them, thus protecting their nectar source. In Australia the cultivated H. aristata appears to be self-pollinating. In the author's garden copious seed is formed without any apparent pollinator being present. Two bird species, the New Holland Honeyeater and the Eastern Spinebill have been seen visiting flowers, as have occasional Honey Bees, but these are likely to be seeking nectar.

The red flowers of Odontonema cuspidatum attract honey-eaters and sunbirds in northern Queensland at least (Odontonema tubaeforme in Discover Nature at JCU, undated, accessed 2020), but whether they are effective pollinators or just robbers of the nectar at the base of the tube is not known. Nor is it known whether fruits are produced and whether seed is also a factor in the spread of this plant. As with many Acanthaceae species they may be effectively spread by vegetative means alone. Comments on this species in the Tropical Garden Society of Sydney indicate that seeds are not produced and it spreads by suckering but this may only apply to more southerly occurrences. A comparative study of nectar-robbing of this species by stingless bees in semi-natural habitat and a coffee plantation in Mexico (Fitch & Vandermeer 2021) is useful for insights into its reproductive biology. Weed risk assessments (Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk 2008; CABI 2020) give this species a high score and cover some of the reproductive biology as part of their attributes scores, but some of the information surrounding seed set may not apply in Australia. Flowers are sometimes of two different sizes on the one shrub at maturity and measurements given in the description are for larger flowers. Larger flowers appear to be homostylous since the style develops to the top of the tube (c. 9--11 mm long) and hence the stigma is at a similar height to the mature anthers. Smaller flowers have tubes 4--7 mm long and lobes c. 3 mm long; they are not cleistogamous as in P. variabile, but heterostylous. In the shorter-tubed flowers the style is either very short (c. 0.5 mm long) or exceeding the anthers by up to 2 mm (see for example, Forster 7850). The number of flowers preserved on specimens is usually small and field work is needed both to confirm these observations and to understand the contribution of these different flower types to the biology and variation of the species. There is at least one record (Phillips 1737, n.v.) of P. tenellum in which the label data indicates its occurrence in the same locality as P. variabile in dry rainforest.

Sanchezia parvibracteata reproduces vegetatively, with broken fragments easily taking root. It also suckers profusely and can form dense thickets under rainforest edges, especially along creeks and other damp, low-lying areas (Queensland Department of Agriculture & Fisheries 2020). Cultivated material is often without fruits overseas but at least one Australian herbarium collection (Gray 6423, n.v.) records their presence, and so seed may also contribute to naturalisation. Most naturalisations are associated with abandoned gardens or abandoned garden waste. In their South American distribution, S. parvibracteata flowers are visited by hummingbirds (Wasshousen & Wood 2004).

Sanchezia parvibracteata has become an environment weed in places. It often forms dense covers in the understory of native and secondary rainforests where it out-competes native plant species (CABI 2020). In Australia S. parvibracteata usually grows in shade in disturbed areas of lowland rainforest and also in the understory of intact rainforest as well as along creek banks (Zich et al. 2020).

While probably native to Brazil, Columbia, Peru and Ecuador in South America, Sanchezia parvibracteata is widely cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions of the world. It is now naturalised in a number of areas including Costa Rica in central America and Hawaii and New Caledonia in the Pacific Ocean. In Australia it is naturalised in the Babinda and Palmerston areas of NE Queensland.

In the absence of seeds, the probable mode of wider dispersal would involve stem fragments and small plantlets (produced at the end of the growing season); these apomicts break off and float away to take root in a suitable location. Dispersal vectors are most likely to be water currents, machinery, boats, water fowl, and people.

For a history of Hydrocleys nymphoides in Australia see Aston & Jacobs (1980) and Kodela & Jobson (2018). There are no records of fruit in the Australian populations, suggesting the possibility it may represent a single clone, or other factors required for fertilisation and seed set are absent (Aston & Jacobs 1980, Kodela & Jobson 2018). However, Hydrocleys nymphoides can reproduce and spread vegetatively, and has the potential to be an invasive weed, particularly in disturbed wetlands and waterways (Aston & Jacobs 1980, Richardson et al. 2011, Romanowski 2011, Randall 2017, Mifsud 2018, Agriculture Victoria 2019, Kodela & Jobson 2018).

Aerva javanica is thought to have been accidentally introduced in the 1880s probably in fodder and saddle packs for the Afghan camel trains. Along with Buffel and Birdwood Grasses (Cenchrus spp.) it was later deliberately introduced to the Ord River catchment area in north-western Western Australia to aid in regeneration of overgrazed and water-eroded areas. Naturalised on Christmas Island. Introduced as a fruit tree, and old trees often mark areas previously cultivated. It is now quite common on the island, and many specimens are self-sown. The natural distribution of Mangifera ×odorata has been obscured through its widespread cultivation throughout Malesia, but it occurs in lowland forest in Sumatra, Java and Borneo.

A second species of mango, Mangifera indica L., is also cultivated on Christmas Island. This species is probably native to India and Burma, but is widely cultivated throughout the tropics, and is commercially the most important mango. The seed produced on Christmas Island is viable and seedlings will grow freely if the fruit is not collected, suggesting that this species may become naturalised in the future. The fruit is delicious eaten raw or dried, and may be used to make pickles, chutney or jam. On Christmas Island, Robber crabs (Birgus latro) gather around fallen palm trees to eat the starchy core of the trunk. In order to collect the crabs for a meal or for fishing bait, an Arenga palm is sometimes felled and the trunk split open, attracting large numbers of crabs a few days later. The crabs also relish the ripe fruit, gathering around the base of a fruiting palm to eat the fruit as it falls, some even climb up to the inflorescences. The fruit is also a favourite of the endemic Christmas Island Imperial Pigeon (Ducula whartoni). It is perhaps surprising that these animals are not affected by the highly irritant sap of the fruit, which contains large quantities of minute sharp crystals which cause intense itching and discomfort if accidentally rubbed into the skin.

Also frequent as an undercanopy tree throughout the taller rainforest on the plateau and terraces, with the juveniles forming important elements of the shrub layer.

A distinctive species, possibly related to Arenga porphyrocarpa (H.Mart.) H.E.Moore or A. microcarpa Becc. Shares the monocarpic habit with A. pinnata, the Sugar Palm (which otherwise differs in many characters), an economically important palm for its sugary sap and the large reserve of starch built up in the trunk prior to flowering and fruiting. Arenga listeri could have similar commercial properties. The female inflorescences sometimes rupture the base of the leaf sheath, but most develop after the leaves have fallen to expose the stem and buds. Typically, the most apical inflorescence is female and develops first. Then the central buds at the nodes develop, again as females, and finally the lateral buds of the nodes develop sequentially into male inflorescences as the tree gradually dies.

Distinguished from perennial species by its smaller flowers, from the perennials and Bulbine alata in having hairs on only 3 stamens, reddish or brownish anthers and smaller capsules, and from B. alata by its wingless seeds. Variable in habit, leaf size and shape, flower size, anther and style orientation and anther colour. Some populations from Tas. and southern coastal mainland appear to be facultatively perennial. The species forms part of a large, taxonomically difficult polyploid complex. Although Bulbine semibarbata and B. alata , the two tetraploid but functionally diploid taxa so far identified at the base of the complex, are differentiated chromosomally and morphologically, intermediates occur over a wide area. These appear to result from some hybridisation and introgression at the 'diploid' level and extensive hybridisation among auto- and allo-polyploid derivatives. Patterns of variation may also have been affected by some cryptic speciation at higher ploidy levels, especially in W.A. In Fl. Centr. Australia 423 (1981), J.P.Jessop distinguished Bulbine semibarbata var. A chiefly on the basis that the pedicels recurved after flowering. Cytological studies show that this character occurs irregularly in disjunct and chromosomally differing populations. Taxonomic segregation on this basis therefore seems inappropriate. It is possible, however, that the Pilbara populations in W.A., where the pedicel is recurved in flower as well as in fruit, may be found to merit separate status.

This Lord Howe Island group is derived from within a clade comprised of numerous Asplenium species including the nest-forming, bird-nest Asplenium (e.g. A. australasicum (J.Sm.) Hook.) and a polyploid species complex in New Zealand and southern Australia that includes A. gracillimum Colenso (Ohlsen et al. 2014; Xu et al. 2020). Apart from Asplenium surrogatum and a dubious count for an Asian species, all chromosome counts reported for species of this large clade are tetraploid or higher (Schneider et al. 2017). This implies that if the diploid count reported for A. surrogatum in Tindale & Roy (2002) is correct it has arisen by a halving a chromosome numbers, which is not yet known in Asplenium, or there has been numerous independent cases of polyploidy from diploid ancestors within this clade (Schneider et al. 2017), which seems unlikely given the lack of putative diploid counts. Consequently, the count reported in Tindale and Roy (2002), which was not supported by an accompanying microphotograph of a squash displaying the chromosomes, is suspect and requires confirmation.

Office of Environment & Heritage (accessed February 2021) for details: https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/threatenedspeciesapp/profile.aspxid=10464 Lepidium peregrinum was previously recorded from the Great Dividing Range, from the Blue Mountains and northeastern New South Wales.

Although native to eastern Australia, Lepidium peregrinum was first discovered as an adventive wool-alien in the British Isles; the type is from Galafoot, Scotland. For a history of the species from its first discovery in the United Kingdom to its connection of origin in Australia, then being presumed extinct and later rediscovered see Scarlett (1999). It is suggested that a sole occurrence of the plant in New Zealand found in 2010 results from the importing of goods directly from Sydney, New South Wales, to Kawhia by Maori during the 1830s to 1860s (Heenan & de Lange 2011). For a more detailed description, notes on leaf form, inflorescences and siliculae, habitat, and diagnostic characters of Lepidium peregrinum and closely related species, see Scarlett (1999).

Sporadically naturalised predominantly through inland Australia south from Alice Springs, but extending south to Melbourne. Present in Western Australia, Northern Territory, South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria. The Victorian occurrence is not substantiated by herbarium specimens, however, plants were observed at Studley Park (Kew) in 1995, by Val Stajsic and G.W. Carr. The natural distribution of Opuntia elatior is uncertain. Hunt et al. (2006) cite the Lesser Antilles, Netherlands Antilles, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama and Venezuela. The species has been widely distributed by humans (Anderson 2001). It is likely to be native to Colombia and Venezuela, but records from Panama and Costa Rica are uncertain, and records from the Caribbean islands may be more recent introductions (Pasiecznik 2015). Opuntia bergeriana, a possible synonym of O. elatior but recognised by some authors (e.g. Innes & Glass 1991), is not known to occur in the wild naturally, but is naturalised in parts of the French and Italian Riviera (Hunt et al. 2006). Hunt et al. (2006) comment that although Opuntia elatior is supposedly a well-known and widespread species, no illustrations of 'typical' O. elatior were available for their publication. They also suggest that it might be masquerading under one or more names provisionally accepted for illustrations (in volume 2 of their publication) for O. pittieri, O. sanguinea, O. schumannii and O. soederstromiana. It's also possible that there is more than one species masquerading under the name Opuntia elatior in Australia.

Stajsic, pers. observ.). The native range is thought to be throughout Europe except in the extreme north but Stellaria media is currently found on every continent, absent only from the Polar Regions and very dry areas. In Australia it occurs in the north from Bundaberg, Queensland, along the east coast and Great Dividing Range through New South Wales to the Victorian coast and mountains, along the Murray floodplain and west to South Australia from Adelaide and surrounding ranges as far west as Port Lincoln. It also occurs on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands, in eastern Tasmania, the Bass Strait Islands and on Macquarie Island. There are a few records for the Northern Territory from Alice Springs, and in Western Australia from coastal areas from Albany to just north of Perth. A single specimen is known from Kununurra in northern Western Australia. There are also scattered occurrences outside these areas in gardens. It is an important economic weed of crops.

The native range of Stellaria pallida extends throughout most of central to western and southern Europe. It has also spread as a weed into the Americas and Asia. Found at scattered localities within New South Wales, along the Great Dividing Range from Tenterfield to Canberra, with one collection inland at Broken Hill. It also occurs along the Murray River drainage system in New South Wales and Victoria. It is found in most areas of Victoria except alpine areas as well as throughout coastal and coastal ranges of South Australia including Kangaroo Island; the northern most collections extend into the Flinders Ranges and the western most collection is at Fowlers Bay near Ceduna. This species is uncommon in Tasmania, being mainly found on offshore islands and in coastal regions but occasionally further inland. It is also uncommon in Western Australia with coastal collections from Rottnest Island and Busselton in the west, Bremer Bay in the south and Cocklebiddy in the east near the South Australian border.

This weed probably has a wider distribution in Australia than listed here but is often overlooked or misidentified as Stellaria media. From examining the herbarium collections it appears S. pallida is a relatively recent introduction to Australia. There are very few collections prior to the 1950s with the earliest collection recorded in 1905 at Tallandoon in Victoria, whereas S. media had been recorded from most states by the mid-1800s. Also see notes under S. media.

Wurmbea inflata has exposed nectaries, which might suggest fly (Dipteran) pollination, although they are not contrastingly coloured as is the case in a number of species. Field observations showed that flies are avid visitors to the flowers of W. inflata and have been observed to probe the nectaries. They are large enough to make contact with the anthers and stigmas and their behaviour is such that pollen transfer is likely. At least two species were observed to visit flowers. However, other visitors have frequently been seen which also are likely pollinators, including two daytime species of Lepidoptera, and two species of bee (Hymenoptera), suggesting that this and perhaps other species of Wurmbea do not have specialised pollinator relationships. A characteristic tree of sandy and rocky beaches; littoral rainforest, beachfront vegetation. On Christmas Island common especially on coastal and upper terraces, often in dense, marginal forest, where it can become one of the largest trees, with massive plank buttresses. On Cocos (Keeling) Islands grows in strand forest in coralline sand, on West and Home Islands, but not common. (Du Puy & Telford 1993: 244).

Ranges from southeast Asia, through Malesia to Polynesia and has been extensively planted throughout the tropics. In Australia it occurs in the extreme northeast of Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, and from islands of Torres Strait to about Mission Beach near Tully, Queensland. Du Puy & Telford (1993: 244) report it is probably native to southeast Asia, extending from India, Indo-China and Malesia to northern Australia and the Pacific islands.

For treatment of Terminalia catappa on Christmas and Cocos (Keeling) Islands see Du Puy & Telford (1993: 243--244). H.N. Ridley, Journal of the Straits Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society 45: 190--191 (1906) noted many very large specimens on Christmas Island, often of greater size than in other localities. It is also unusual for this species to occur naturally above the littoral zone. The leaves are deciduous, turning first yellow and then bright red before falling. (Du Puy & Telford 1993: 244).

Restricted to southwestern Victoria and adjoining regions of South Australia and New South Wales. Sutter (2010) confirms the species from three locations - in the Mereek Flora Reserve near Edenhope (Victoria); in the Little Desert National Park along the Border Track (Victoria), and on adjoining private land at Bangham (South Australia); and a single 1987 record from the Grampians National Park near Woohlpooer (Victoria). Widespread from the Kimberley, Western Australia, to the Northern Territory and Queensland. In the Northern Territory recorded from the Victoria River region (Fitzmaurice River, Jasper Gorge), Daly Basin, Nitmiluk National Park, Pine Creek, Arnhem Land and Barkly Tableland (Elliot and Tennant Creek). Probably extinct in the MacDonnell Ranges.

The interpretation of the degree of fusion of the male sepals is difficult in this species. Most material from Queensland and the Northern Territory shows apparently free male sepals but with some degree of fusion at the base. Material from the Kimberley mostly has the sepals fused into a spathe which is typically deeply divided. This considerable variation could all represent derivations from a 3-lobed spathe which has become variously divided. The most typical form is two free sepals as seen in the Banks & Solander type specimen, but one and three free sepals have been also observed. The observation that these are often fused at the base supports that these could all be derived from a deeply divided spathe. The observation of one sepal could also be that of a very narrow spathe.

Grows in permanent or semi-permanent freshwater bodies such as waterholes, running streams or standing water in Melaleuca swamps, open forests or sedge/grasslands, floodplains and sandstone pavements; in full sun or shaded situations. Also survives on drying margins.

Widespread from Africa, India, SE Asia, New Guinea and Australia; occurs in northern Australia from the Kimberley, Western Australia, Top End, Northern Territory, Gulf of Carpentaria and north Queensland.

Fruit and seed dispersal in Eriocaulon setaceum appears quite different to other species of Eriocaulon. In other species the ovary is readily dehiscent and the seeds are released through a loculicidal opening in the ovary wall while the female flower is within the capitulum. In E. setaceum the ovary is tardily dehiscent and the entire 3-merous ovary is shed from the capitulum with the seeds retained within the ovary locules. The ovary is buoyant and appears to function as the diaspore unit. Eventually the loculicidal slit opens and releases the seeds which are covered in mucilage and appear to sink soon after release. Ramaswarmy et al. (1983) reported in various species of Eriocaulon that the cells of the inner layer of the ovary wall develop band-like thickenings which they suggest help in the dehiscence of the fruit. They note these bands are absent in E. setaceum which may explain the tardy dehiscence.

Sporadically recorded as escaping in New South Wales, e.g. Cooma and Yass Valley (Lohr & Keighery 2016), and Lake George (viz. Purdie 8053, CANB, NSW). Adventive records in the Australian Capital Territory involve one of two individuals, often with some seedlings and/or occasionally saplings; these are currently not considered populations of self-sustaining individuals, hence Quercus robur is not regarded as naturalised in the territory (B.J. Tannic acid in the leaves is poisonous to horses if consumed in excess, while the acorns are poisonous to horses and cattle, though pigs can consume them safely in moderation (Quercus robur, in Plants of the World Online, accessed 5 April 2022). A common street and park tree in Canberra assigned the name Quercus lusitanica (e.g. Edwards 1979, Pryor & Banks 2001: 148) looks superficially similar to Q. robur but differs in having more regular and usually less deeply lobed leaves with (5-) 6--8 lobes each side, and regular more acute secondary veins. However, these trees have rounded lobes while Quercus lusitanica has pointed acute to obtuse lobes/teeth.

Corolla yellow with brownish lines. As is common with such a wide-ranging species there is considerable variation. Several authors have been impressed by the difference in flower (and plant) size, e.g., E.Pritzel who described Calogyne berardiana var. major and S.Moore who described Calogyne linearis , based on small-flowered short forms. The large-flowered forms occur in the more northerly parts of the range whilst the small-flowered forms also occur in the east and south-east. In the Albany-Stirling Ra. region, a form with intermediate-sized flowers occurs. Where the small- and large-flowered forms occur together, other characteristics of the two forms are the same. For example specimens from Taillifer Isthmus, Shark Bay, have glabrous stems; and at the mouth of the Murchison R. they are similar in indumentum. At these two localities the two forms grow in the same populations. The implication is that the large and small-flowered states occur in the same population either as a phenotypic expression or as a genetic polymorphism. The indumentum is another feature that shows considerable variation. All specimens have both simple and glandular hairs but the proportions vary, best observed on the undersurface of the leaves. In the eastern specimens almost all the hairs in this position are glandular, while the proportion of simple hairs increases towards the west reaching its highest value in specimens from parts of the Goldfields region of W.A.

Occurs in temperate areas of W.A., Qld, N.S.W. and Vic. Possibly on Eyre Peninsula, S.A., fide J.P.Jessop & H.R.Toelken (eds), Fl. S. Australia 4th edn, 1768 (1986).

An extremely variable species which on presently available herbarium material cannot unequivocally be subdivided, though extreme forms are very distinctive. Some have been treated as species but many specimens show intermediate characters or both states of so-called distinctions. W.A. material (or parts of it) may be subspecifically or specifically distinct from eastern and south-eastern material. Plants in W.A. are considered toxic to livestock and one form has been proven such, but in eastern Australia plants are not considered toxic. The two groups apparently have different chromosome numbers. Three counts from widely differing plants in W.A. were all n = 16, whereas two counts from south-eastern Qld plants were both n = 8. Cave's material, grown from seed gathered near Canberra, was also n = 8. The species is worthy of closer study. The names Stypandra imbricata and S. grandiflora were applied to young or old low plants with medium to broad leaf laminas in south-western W.A.; S. virgata was applied to older, taller plants with narrow leaf laminas and S. scoparia to old tall plants with short filiform leaves in this same region. S. propinqua , applied to young plants with comparatively narrow leaves, and S. latifolia , to young plants with very broad leaves occurring in eastern Australia, are unquestionably synomyns of S. glauca . Stypandra glauca has been recorded by various authors as occurring in New Caledonia, e.g. A.Guillaumin, Flore analytique et synoptique de la Nouvelle-Caledonie 54 (1948). This record is apparently based on a specimen in Paris herbarium labelled as collected from New Caledonia by R.S.Montrouzier in 1868 (photo BRI). Though the material is not complete, there seems no doubt that it is correctly identified. The species apparently has not been collected in New Caledonia this century.

Occurs sporadically in coastal and subcoastal northern Australia from Walcott Inlet, Western Australia, across northern Northern Territory, to near Gayndah, Queensland. Inland populations appear to be variants, localised or perhaps clinal, and are discussed below. The pantropical strand form is widespread in tropical America and Asia, Malesia, the western Pacific and northern Indian Oceans, including Christmas and Cocos (Keeling) Islands. On Christmas Island, common on the lower terraces, forming part of the canopy of open forest. Recorded for Cocos (Keeling) Island by K. Kubitzki in H.G.A. Engler, Bot. Jahrb. Syst. 89: 183 (1969), where a collection by D. Prain, 1890, is cited. The species has not been collected there since.

Inland populations occur in the western Kimberley, Western Australia, northern Northern Territory and in central Queensland. The Kimberley trees, e.g. Edkins Range, c. 132 km from 'Mt Elizabeth' Homestead along Walcott Inlet track, I.R. Telford 11625 (CBG, DNA, PERTH); Isdell River, May 1983 D.G. Fell (BRI, PERTH), bear leaves more densely hairy above and with denser crisped hairs on the veins on the undersurface, similar to subsp. sphenopterus but with grey, not yellowish hairs. These occur near Walcott Inlet in woodland on sandstone outcrops to 450 m altitude. Those of the Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, escarpment, e.g. Kakadu National Park, 0.5 km E of Koongarra Saddle, I.R. Telford 11684 & J. Palmer (BISH, BRI, CBG, DNA, MO, PERTH); Ja Ja Creek, near Cannon Hill, H.S. Thompson 341 (CBG), more closely resemble the strand form, but differ in the very short indumentum of the leaf undersurface. They grow in monsoon rainforest with Allosyncarpia ternata, Planchonella arnhemica and Myristica insipida, in gullies of sandstone escarpments to 250 m altitude. Some northern Queensland populations, e.g. 0.5 km NW of 'Toomba' Homestead, Great Basalt Wall, P.I. Forster 3677 (BRI, CBG), resemble the Kimberley and Arnhem Land populations. This geographic variation requires more detailed investigation. A variant with darker, more dense and more durable wood is also reported from Christmas Island. The trunk of these specimens is reddish, marred by outgrowths on the lower part, suggesting an abnormality due to insect or fungal attack.

Grows in wet areas. In its native range Triadenum japonicum grows in wet meadows and marshes, on lowlands and hillsides (Robson 2006). In Australia it has been recorded growing in dark brown silt over sandstone at the edge of a swamp, and in black peaty soil on sediment in a Carex sedgeland.
Native of Japan, Korea, China and eastern Russia. In Australia only known from a swamp at Dubbo Gully near Mangrove Mountain, and in Werrikimbe National Park, New South Wales.

Triadenum japonicum has possibly escaped or spread from past cultivation of plants at or near the sites it has been recorded; “Mooraback” is an old grazing property with a homestead and remnant garden plants near Bishop Swamp, and at Dubbo Gully there was an old settlement nearby (John Hosking, pers. comm., February 2019).

The hermaphroditic flowers of P. conniana are protandrous (Wilson et al. 2017). During early anthesis (male phase), the fertile anthers are positioned next to the inner adaxial surface of the corolla. The female phase begins when the style becomes incurved, the stigma lobes part and become receptive, and the stamens begin senescing as they reposition laterally to the side of the inner surface of the corolla. The pollinators of P. conniana are poorly known. We have observed visits to P. conniana by syrphids and other small species of Diptera, Lepidoptera, and small Coleoptera; however, it is likely that only syrphid flies are able to contact anthers and transfer pollen. The floral morphology and corolla markings are consistent with flowers of other Prostanthera that have been observed by us to be pollinated by small bees and flies similar to the size of syrphids.

Prostanthera conniana is known only from a few sites over an area of 5 km2 within the Shoalhaven Gorge of Bungonia State Conservation Area, New South Wales, Australia (Fig. 4 in Wilson et al. 2015). In general, the northern populations (those in the wetter parts of Qld) tend to be larger, with larger, broader leaves that usually have a slightly revolute margin; those throughout much of N.S.W. are medium in size, with medium-sized, flat to revolute leaves; whereas the Vic. populations are usually small with smaller revolute leaves. Hibiscus kirstyae is restricted to ridges away from the pavement margins, presumably to afford them some degree of protection from fire. The type population consists of around 200 individuals that are estimated to live for 3--6 years between fire periods.

Occurs on two large sandstone pavements 15 km apart near the Morgan River on Theda Station, Western Australia. Each pavement is 0.9--1.2 km long and c. 300 m wide, however, the Hibiscus kirstyae populations occupy only a portion of each pavement.

Considerable effort has been undertaken to locate additional populations in the region over a period of 12 years, including extensive observations by helicopter, but no further populations have been located to date. The glabrous capsule is unusual amongst Australian indigenous species, shared only with Hibiscus meraukensis Hochr., which is distinguished from H. kirstyae by having deeply 2- or 3-lobed leaves, longer epicalyx lobes more than half as long as the calyx lobes, and white petals. From a distance the glaucous leaves, yellow flowers and tall shrub habit have the appearance of a Calotropis R.Br. with yellow deciduous leaves, which are noxious weeds elsewhere in the Kimberley.

A collection in MEL (Palmer s.n., Queensland, Mitchell River, 1882) may represent this species. A preliminary molecular phylogeny of sect. Trichospermum indicates the New Guinean and Australian H. panduriformis is conspecific.

Hibiscus saponarius seems to be most closely related to H. meraukensis. Both species have acuminate calyx lobes that are glabrous except on the ribs. The capsules of H. saponarius are sparsely pubescent, those of H. meraukensis are glabrous to sparsely pubescent, in contrast to all other Australian species which have densely pubescent capsules. The branchlets of H. meraukensis are usually glabrous or have recurved aculei but two collections examined (Clarkson 6471, 6934 & Neldner, BRI, CANB) have hairs similar to those on H. saponarius except that they are shorter and not quite as dense. Clarkson 6934 & Neldner appears to be from a small, trailing plant and has a glabrous capsule; Clarkson 6471 & Neldner was described as a trailing shrub and has a sparsely pubescent capsule. All other collections of H. meraukensis seen from Queensland represent the typical, non-stellate-pubescent, aculeate form of the species.

Northern and eastern Australia from the Kimberley region, Western Australia, through the Northern Territory and Queensland S to Milton, New South Wales, but original distribution completely obscured by cultivated and naturalised forms (see below). Certainly naturalised in SW Western Australia, South Australia, Victoria and possibly Tasmania. Also in drier Indomalesia from India and Nepal, Sri Lanka and tropical China to Solomon Islands.

This species is a complex of wild and cultivated forms, discussed by D.J. Mabberley, Gardens' Bulletin Singapore 37: 49--64 (1984). The wild plants in Australia often have more distinctly pink or even mauve flowers than those further west and those from Java eastwards including Australia are often less stellate-hairy than those to the west. The leaflets of apparently truly wild plants in Australia are entire and drupes are up to 4 cm long. Selected precocious forms have been grown for over 2500 years and may be grouped as Indian and Chinese cultivars, the former of which have been introduced throughout the warmer parts of the world, where they are widely naturalised and can become a nuisance. This is the Persian or Cape Lilac which is widely cultivated in Australia as an ornamental and as a street tree. Also cultivated are Australian strains, which prove remarkably adaptable to the dry conditions of inland stations. Hybrids between different cultivars occur in cultivation and, in Australia, both exotic and native plants have become naturalised within and beyond the putative natural distribution of the species. Around Perth and Adelaide the weedy forms appear to be Persian Lilac, whereas elsewhere it is often difficult to pigeon hole the naturalised plants. Distinctive named cultivars include ‘Floribunda’, which flowers when less than 50 cm tall, and ‘Umbraculifera’, the ‘Texas Umbrella Tree’, a mutant form with a flattened crown of branches, first selected in Texas in the nineteenth century. Fast-growing cultivars have been selected for plantation work, particularly in S America. Timber is used for furniture and light construction such as ceilings, boats, tea chests, also as fibre board and in paper making. It is grown as coffee shade but the fruit is toxic to pigs and humans (6--8 a fatal dose in children) and cows fed on the leaves yield tainted milk. The toxic principles are limonoids - meliatoxins A1, A2, B1, B2 (P.B. Oelrichs et al., Phytochemistry 22: 531--534 (1983)). The insecticidal qualities of the leaves have long been recognised in China and India and are now being appreciated elsewhere. A steroid ester, azedarachol, isolated from root-bark has been found efficacious in Japan (M. Nakatani et al., Phytochemistry 24: 1945--1948 (1985)). In China the seed-oil has been found to be quite effective as an antifeedant to yellow rice-borers, but not striped or pink ones, and similarly effective against white-backed and brown planthoppers but not leafhoppers or rice thrips (J. Hu et al., Journal of the Agricultural Association of China Nanking 1983: 63--69 (1983)). The oil is also effective in control of certain citrus pests, while powdered ripe seeds or leaves are mixed with stored wheat to preserve it from insect attack (W. & H. Olkowski, IPM Practitioner 10: 1--6 (1988)). A glycopeptide, meliacin, isolated from the leaves and roots, is responsible for inhibition of in-vitro replication of various DNA and RNA animal viruses (G.M. Andrei et al., Antiviral Research 9: 221--231 (1988)). It also triggers an antiviral state in cells prior to infection and, although the mechanism is not like that in interferon, it is otherwise not understood. Further medical uses are discussed by Mabberley et al., Flora Melesiana series 1, 12 (1995).

Because the tree is deciduous, its tree-rings have potential in reconstructing early season temperatures and late-season rainfall patterns of the past (see I. Heinrich & J.C.G. Banks, Australian Journal of Botany 53: 21--32 (2005)). Possibly the most prized of all Australian native timbers, red cedar has been logged so effectively that good specimens are now rare. Trees over 60 m tall have been recorded and some idea of their value and exploitation for furniture, coach-building, doors and other joinery can be gained from the Post-War daily press (see, e.g. P.J. Hurley, Sydney Morning Herald 1 November 1947), recording the disappearance of these gigantic trees, of which even the roots were valued (for a popular illustrated account see J. Vader, Red Cedar: The Tree of Australia's History (1987)). Flowering in spring, red cedar is sometimes cultivated for ornament but it is difficult to grow in plantation because, like other Meliaceae, it is prone to devastating attacks by shoot borers (Hypsipyla robusta). In the neotropics, these moths are attracted by a chemical allied to substances which, in species from other parts of the world, are toxic to the local moths. Thus, T. ciliata is resistant to attack in Costa Rica and it is alleged that this resistance may be transferred to the susceptible local Cedrela odorata L. if a scion of it is grafted on to a stock of Toona. There have been many attempts at biological control of the moths, for externally applied insecticides have little effect and systemic ones are expensive.
